children: Every festive season, the conversation around Indian commerce turns to the same things: how much consumers will spend, which categories will see the biggest surge and whether businesses are ready for the rush.
But there is another question worth asking. What does the festive season reveal about the businesses that are participating in it?

For India's MSMEs, the festive period is no longer simply a few weeks of elevated demand. It is a stress test of the entire business. Inventory, fulfilment, logistics, customer experience and technology are all tested simultaneously. When demand rises sharply, the gaps that remain invisible during ordinary months become difficult to ignore.

That is why I increasingly see festive preparation not as a seasonal exercise, but as a measure of business readiness. A merchant that can sell more but cannot fulfil reliably has not really scaled. A business that can acquire customers across multiple channels but cannot maintain inventory visibility across those channels has created demand without building the infrastructure to meet it. And a brand that can build strong domestic demand but cannot navigate the complexity of international commerce may find that its ambitions have outgrown its operating model.
The Right Stock, In The Right Place

The first challenge is still inventory, but the question has changed. The traditional approach was to look at historical sales and add a buffer for the festive season. That becomes increasingly inadequate as commerce becomes more regional, fragmented and dynamic. Demand can vary significantly by geography, category and channel. What sells rapidly in one market may move differently in another.

The ability to understand these patterns and position inventory accordingly is becoming a competitive advantage. The objective is not to hold more stock. It is about having the right stock in the right location at the right time.

The same principle applies to the way merchants reach customers. Today's consumer does not think in channels. A product may be discovered on social media, evaluated on a marketplace, purchased through a brand's own website and returned through a completely different process. For the merchant, however, every additional channel can introduce another layer of operational complexity.

The businesses that scale will therefore be those that make this complexity invisible. They will need a common view of inventory, integrated fulfilment and the ability to serve demand wherever it originates. This is particularly important during festive peaks, when every additional manual process gets amplified.

Logistics is perhaps where this becomes most visible. Peak demand can change the economics and performance of a delivery network almost overnight. A courier that is the right choice for one route may not be the right choice for another. Capacity changes. Delivery density changes. Serviceability changes. Even the reliability of a particular route can shift during a peak.
This is why the next evolution in logistics is not simply about adding more delivery capacity. It is about making better decisions with the capacity that already exists.

Intelligent routing, real-time network signals, and dynamic fulfilment can enable a business to decide not merely whether an order can be delivered, but also how it should be delivered. Increasingly, even the delivery promise shown to a customer at checkout is connected to these underlying decisions.
That is an important shift. Logistics is moving upstream, from a post-purchase function to part of the commerce proposition itself.
From Local Businesses To Global Commerce

But perhaps the most interesting change is happening beyond India's domestic market. For years, the natural progression for an MSME was to move from a local market to a larger city, then to national marketplaces and eventually to a national customer base. Technology is beginning to compress that journey.

A merchant that can build a brand in India can increasingly find customers in Dubai, London, Singapore or New York without first having to build a physical presence in each market. What stands between that merchant and global demand is often not demand itself, but complexity.

Cross-border commerce brings customs, documentation, duties, carrier selection, shipping modes, tracking and destination-market requirements into the equation. Historically, managing that complexity required specialist teams and relationships that were difficult for a small business to build. Technology is changing that equation. Just as a merchant should not have to build its own logistics network to serve a customer in Bengaluru, it should not have to become an international logistics expert to serve a customer in London. The infrastructure should absorb that complexity.
This is why I believe the next phase of India's MSME growth will be defined not simply by how many businesses sell online, but by how many can build businesses without being constrained by geography.
The Festive Rush

The festive season is a useful lens into this transition because it compresses the test. Can a business handle a sudden increase in demand? Can it maintain the customer experience across channels? Can its inventory and fulfilment systems respond quickly? Can its technology reduce complexity rather than add to it? And perhaps most importantly, can the operating model built to handle today's demand support tomorrow's ambition? That ambition may be national. Increasingly, it may also be global.

The infrastructure available to an MSME today is fundamentally different from what was available even a few years ago. Technology is allowing smaller businesses to access capabilities that once required considerable scale: integrated commerce channels, distributed fulfilment, intelligent logistics, automated workflows and cross-border shipping infrastructure.

This changes the meaning of being an MSME. Being small in employee count or physical footprint does not necessarily mean thinking small geographically. A business can be born in a neighbourhood, build demand across India, and increasingly serve customers around the world, provided the underlying infrastructure can scale to meet that ambition.

That is the opportunity I see in the festive season. The real winners will not necessarily be the businesses that process the most orders during a few high-demand weeks. They will be the ones that use the pressure of the season to build a business capable of handling whatever comes next.
The ultimate test of festive readiness is not whether a business can survive the rush. It is whether, when the rush is over, it is ready to go further.
Akshay Ghulati
Guest Author Akshay Ghulati, Co-founder, Shiprocket.
